content: The initial management of shoulder dystocia involves performing specific maneuvers designed to alleviate the obstruction by adjusting the position of the fetal shoulders and expanding the effective dimensions of the maternal pelvis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of prophylactic maneuvers in preventing shoulder dystocia. A search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of May 2009. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared the use of prophylactic maneuvers and maternal positioning with standard or routine care. Two authors independently applied exclusion criteria, assessed the quality of the trials, and extracted relevant data. Two trials were included in the review. The first trial compared the McRobert's maneuver combined with suprapubic pressure to no prophylactic maneuvers in 185 women who were at risk of delivering a large baby. The second trial compared the McRobert's maneuver to lithotomy positioning in 40 women. The results of these two trials were not pooled due to differences in their methodologies. In the first study, 15 cases of shoulder dystocia were reported in the control group, compared to five cases in the prophylactic group. This corresponded to a risk ratio (RR) of 0.44, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0.17 to 1.14. The second study reported one case of shoulder dystocia in both the prophylactic and lithotomy groups. In the first study, the prophylactic group had a significantly higher rate of cesarean sections. When these cesarean deliveries were included in the analysis, the prophylactic group demonstrated significantly fewer cases of shoulder dystocia, with an RR of 0.33 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.86). Additionally, in this study, 13 women in the control group required therapeutic maneuvers after the delivery of the fetal head, compared to three women in the prophylactic group (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.02). One study reported no instances of birth injuries or low Apgar scores. In the other study, one infant in the control group experienced a brachial plexus injury (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.02 to 10.61), and one infant had a five-minute Apgar score below seven (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.02 to 10.61). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to definitively support or oppose the use of prophylactic maneuvers to prevent shoulder dystocia. While one study indicated an increased rate of cesarean sections in the prophylactic group, both studies failed to address critical maternal outcomes, such as maternal injuries, psychological effects, and satisfaction with the birthing experience. Given the low incidence of shoulder dystocia, larger trials are necessary to investigate the effectiveness of these maneuvers.
